los.text: Label a diagrammatic sketch of the structure of a tooth
los.html:
PartDetail
CrownAbove the gum, covered by enamel (hardest tissue in the body; acellular, can't repair)
NeckWhere enamel meets cementum
RootIn the socket, covered by cementum
DentineBulk of the tooth under enamel and cementum; sensitive (tubules)
Pulp cavityPulp chamber + root canal: nerves, vessels, connective tissue; enters at the apical foramen
Periodontal ligamentFixes the root in the alveolar bone (gomphosis)
GingivaGum around the neck

los.text: Recall the order and timings of tooth eruption
los.html:
DentitionEruptsOrder
Deciduous (20)~6 months to ~2½ years
  • Central incisors (6–10 months, lower first)
  • → lateral incisors
  • → first molars (~12–16 months)
  • → canines (~16–20 months)
  • → second molars (~20–30 months)
Permanent (32)~6 years onwards
  • First molars (6 years)
  • Central incisors (6–8)
  • Lateral incisors (7–9)
  • Canines (9–12) and premolars (10–12)
  • Second molars (12 years)
  • Third molars (17–25 years, "wisdom teeth")
Mixed dentition~6–12 years.
Delayed eruptionHypothyroidism, rickets, Down syndrome.

los.text: Describe the arrangement of the dentition
los.html:
DeciduousPermanent
Per quadrant2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 molars (5)2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars (8)
Total2032
Formula2-1-0-22-1-2-3
Notation (Palmer/FDI)
  • Teeth numbered 1–8 from the midline in each quadrant (FDI adds the quadrant number: e.g. 11 = upper right central incisor)
  • Deciduous teeth lettered A–E.
ArrangementUpper and lower arches; incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Permanent premolars replace deciduous molars.

los.text: Identify the parts of the mandible
los.html:
PartFeatures
BodyAlveolar part (teeth), mental protuberance, mental foramen (below the 2nd premolar: mental nerve), mylohyoid line inside, digastric fossa, genial tubercles
RamusVertical; mandibular foramen on the inner surface (inferior alveolar nerve and vessels enter) guarded by the lingula (sphenomandibular ligament)
AngleWhere body meets ramus; masseter (outside) and medial pterygoid (inside) attach
Coronoid processFront of the ramus; temporalis attaches
Condylar processHead + neck; head in the TMJ; lateral pterygoid attaches to the neck
Mandibular notchBetween coronoid and condyle (masseteric nerve and vessels)
  • Fractures: often in two places (ring), commonly the condylar neck and the opposite angle or body.

los.text: Name the boundaries of the temporal fossa
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
Upper / posteriorSuperior temporal line (temporal fascia)
Lower (lateral)Zygomatic arch
FrontFrontal process of zygoma, zygomatic process of frontal bone
Floor (medial wall)Parts of the frontal, parietal, temporal and greater wing of sphenoid (meeting at the pterion)
RoofTemporal fascia
Pterion
  • The thinnest part of the skull
  • The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies beneath → fracture causes an extradural haematoma.
ContentsTemporalis, deep temporal nerves and vessels; continuous below the arch with the infratemporal fossa.

los.text: Identify and describe the temporalis muscle and locate the auriculotemporal nerve and the superficial temporal blood vessels
los.html:
Temporalis
  • Fan-shaped
  • From the floor of the temporal fossa and temporal fascia → coronoid process and front of the ramus.
  • Elevates the mandible (closes the jaw)
  • Posterior fibres retract it.
  • Nerve: deep temporal nerves (V3).
Auriculotemporal nerve(V3)
  • Splits round the middle meningeal artery → behind the TMJ → up in front of the ear with the superficial temporal vessels.
  • Sensation to the temple and auricle
  • Carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid (from IX via the otic ganglion) → Frey's syndrome after parotidectomy (gustatory sweating).
Superficial temporal arteryTerminal branch of the ECA; pulse in front of the tragus; tender and thickened in giant cell arteritis (biopsy site).
Order in front of the ear(back → front)Auriculotemporal nerve, superficial temporal vein, superficial temporal artery.

los.text: Identify the temporomandibular joint, the components of the joint and the accessory ligaments (temporomandibular, sphenomandibular, stylomandibular)
los.html:
• TMJ: synovial joint between the head of the mandible and the mandibular fossa and articular eminence of the temporal bone, divided by a fibrocartilage articular disc into upper and lower compartments.
CompartmentMovement
Upper (disc–temporal bone)Gliding (protrusion, translation)
Lower (head–disc)Hinge (rotation)
  • Capsule: loose above, tighter below; lateral pterygoid inserts into the disc and the neck of the mandible.
LigamentAttachmentsRole
Lateral (temporomandibular)Articular tubercle → neck of mandibleMain stabiliser; stops backward displacement
SphenomandibularSpine of sphenoid → lingulaAccessory; inferior alveolar nerve passes between it and the ramus
StylomandibularStyloid process → angle of mandibleAccessory; limits protrusion
  • Fibrocartilage (not hyaline) covers the articular surfaces: it develops from membrane bone.

los.text: Recall the movements that can occur during chewing and name the muscles involved in each movement
los.html:
MovementMuscles
Elevation (close)Temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid
Depression (open)Lateral pterygoid (starts it, pulls the condyle forward) + gravity, digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid
ProtrusionLateral and medial pterygoids (both sides)
RetractionPosterior fibres of temporalis
Side-to-side (grinding)Lateral and medial pterygoids of one side pull that side forward, so the chin moves to the opposite side
  • Opening: first the head rotates in the lower compartment (hinge), then the head and disc glide forward onto the articular eminence (upper compartment).

los.text: Explain what occurs in anterior temporomandibular joint dislocation and relocation
los.html:
Anterior dislocation
  • on wide opening (yawn, blow)
  • The head of the mandible slides in front of the articular eminence and gets stuck there
  • Held by spasm of masseter
  • Temporalis and medial pterygoid.
  • The mouth is stuck open
  • Often bilateral.
Relocation
  • Thumbs (wrapped) on the lower molars, press down (to clear the eminence) then back
  • Then the elevators snap the jaw shut (so protect the thumbs).
RiskFacial nerve and auriculotemporal nerve stretch; recurrent dislocation with lax ligaments.

los.text: Name the muscles of mastication, their origins and insertions, actions and innervation (masseter, temporalis, lateral and medial pterygoid muscles)
los.html:
MuscleOriginInsertionActionNerve
MasseterZygomatic archLateral surface of ramus and angleElevates, slight protrusionMasseteric (V3)
TemporalisTemporal fossaCoronoid processElevates, retracts (posterior fibres)Deep temporal (V3)
Medial pterygoidMedial surface of lateral pterygoid plate (deep head), maxillary tuberosityMedial surface of ramus and angleElevates, protrudes, side-to-sideV3
Lateral pterygoidLateral surface of lateral pterygoid plate, greater wing of sphenoidNeck of mandible, disc and capsuleOpens the jaw, protrudes, side-to-sideV3
  • All supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3), the only motor part of the trigeminal
    • all come from the 1st pharyngeal arch.
  • V3 lesion: weak bite, the jaw deviates towards the weak side on opening (unopposed opposite lateral pterygoid).

los.text: Locate the infratemporal fossa and name its boundaries
los.html:
• Infratemporal fossa: below the temporal fossa, deep to the ramus.
BoundaryFormed by
LateralRamus of the mandible
MedialLateral pterygoid plate
FrontBack of the maxilla
RoofGreater wing of sphenoid (with foramen ovale and spinosum)
BackStyloid process, carotid sheath
FloorOpen (where medial pterygoid attaches to the angle)
Contents
  • Lateral and medial pterygoids
  • Maxillary artery (with the middle meningeal branch)
  • Pterygoid venous plexus
  • Mandibular nerve (inferior alveolar, lingual, buccal, auriculotemporal)
  • Chorda tympani joining the lingual nerve
  • Otic ganglion.
ClinicalInferior alveolar nerve block; the pterygoid plexus links to the cavernous sinus (spread of infection).

los.text: Recognise the major bones of the skull, including the frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal, maxilla, zygoma, mandible, sphenoid, nasal and ethmoid bones and identify their surface and imaging landmarks
los.html:
BoneLandmarks
FrontalForehead, supraorbital margin and notch, frontal sinus, roof of orbits
Parietal (2)Vault; temporal lines; grooved inside by middle meningeal vessels
OccipitalForamen magnum, occipital condyles, external occipital protuberance, superior nuchal line
Temporal (2)Squamous part, zygomatic process, mastoid process (air cells), styloid process, external acoustic meatus, petrous part (inner ear), mandibular fossa
SphenoidBody (sella turcica, sphenoid sinus), greater and lesser wings, pterygoid plates; many foramina
EthmoidCribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate (septum), ethmoid air cells, thin medial orbital wall
Maxilla (2)Upper jaw, maxillary sinus, infraorbital foramen, hard palate (front), alveolar process
Zygoma (2)Cheekbone; zygomatic arch with the temporal bone; lateral orbital wall
Nasal (2)Bridge of the nose
MandibleLower jaw (the only movable skull bone)
Imagingon skull X-rays and CT, identify the sinuses, sella, mastoid air cells, orbits, sutures and vascular grooves (don't mistake them for fractures).
Bones forming the pterionFrontal, parietal, temporal, sphenoid.

los.text: Identify the major sutural joints of the adult skull and the fontanelles of the foetal skull
los.html:
SutureBetween
CoronalFrontal and both parietals
SagittalTwo parietals
LambdoidParietals and occipital
SquamousParietal and temporal
MetopicTwo halves of the frontal boneUsually fuses by ~1 year
  • Bregma: meeting of coronal and sagittal sutures. Lambda: meeting of sagittal and lambdoid.
FontanellePositionCloses
AnteriorDiamond, at the bregma~18 months
PosteriorTriangle, at the lambda~2–3 months
Sphenoidal and mastoid (pairs)SidesFirst year
  • Clinical: bulging anterior fontanelle = raised ICP (meningitis)
    • sunken = dehydration.
    • Overlapping sutures allow moulding in birth.
    • Craniosynostosis: early fusion → abnormal head shape.

los.text: Identify the external and internal features of the cranial foramina of the skull, the bones through which they pass, listing the structures that each transmits
los.html:
ForamenBoneTransmits
Cribriform plateEthmoidOlfactory nerves (I)
Optic canalSphenoid (lesser wing)Optic nerve (II), ophthalmic artery
Superior orbital fissureSphenoid (between wings)III, IV, V1, VI, superior ophthalmic vein
Foramen rotundumSphenoid (greater wing)Maxillary nerve (V2)
Foramen ovaleSphenoid (greater wing)Mandibular nerve (V3), lesser petrosal nerve, emissary veins
Foramen spinosumSphenoid (greater wing)Middle meningeal artery
Foramen lacerumSphenoid/temporal/occipitalFilled with cartilage; ICA passes over it
Carotid canalTemporal (petrous)Internal carotid artery, sympathetic plexus
Internal acoustic meatusTemporal (petrous)VII, VIII, labyrinthine artery
Stylomastoid foramenTemporalFacial nerve (VII) leaving the skull
Jugular foramenTemporal/occipitalIX, X, XI, internal jugular vein (sigmoid sinus), inferior petrosal sinus
Hypoglossal canalOccipitalXII
Foramen magnumOccipitalMedulla/spinal cord, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of XI, meninges
Infraorbital foramenMaxillaInfraorbital nerve (V2) and vessels
Mental foramenMandibleMental nerve (V3) and vessels
Supraorbital notchFrontalSupraorbital nerve (V1)

los.text: Describe the blood supply and nervous innervation of the teeth
los.html:
TeethNerveBranch ofArtery
Upper (maxillary)Superior alveolar nerves (posterior, middle, anterior)Maxillary (V2) (posterior directly; middle and anterior via the infraorbital nerve)Superior alveolar arteries (maxillary artery)
Lower (mandibular)Inferior alveolar nerve (→ mental and incisive branches)Mandibular (V3)Inferior alveolar artery (maxillary artery)
GumsUpper buccal (superior alveolar, infraorbital), upper palatal (greater palatine, nasopalatine); lower lingual (lingual nerve), lower buccal (buccal, mental nerves).
Veinsto the pterygoid plexus and facial vein. Lymph: submandibular nodes (lower incisors: submental).
Clinical
  • Inferior alveolar nerve block numbs all the lower teeth on one side, the lower lip and chin (mental nerve) and often the tongue (lingual nerve nearby).
  • Upper teeth can be infiltrated locally because the maxilla is thin and porous.
  • Upper molar roots lie close to the maxillary sinus, so sinusitis can cause toothache.
